nameStory: The "Powder-tipped Starburst" name captures this lichen's dramatic appearance perfectly. Its leaf-like lobes radiate outward like a starburst or flower, and the tips are often dusted with a fine, powdery substance called soredia that looks like it's been sprinkled with flour. When you spot one spreading across tree bark, it really does look like nature created its own tiny firework display.
description: Powder-tipped Starburst Lichen is a foliose (leafy) lichen that forms rosettes or irregular patches on tree bark. It has gray-green to bluish-gray lobes that spread outward from the center, typically growing 2-4 inches across. The most distinctive feature is the powdery white or pale soredia that dust the lobe tips, giving it a frosted appearance. This medium-sized lichen creates attractive patterns as it slowly expands across its host tree.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for powdery white or pale soredia dusting the lobe tips - run your finger gently over them and you'll feel the fine, flour-like texture that easily rubs off

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms leafy rosettes with lobes radiating outward like petals of a flower, creating starburst patterns on bark

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to bluish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found growing on the bark of coniferous trees, especially spruces and firs in acidic forest environments

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches typically measure 2-4 inches across, with lobes extending about half an inch from the center

habitat: This lichen favors the bark of coniferous trees in cool, moist forests throughout New England's mountains and northern regions. You'll most often find it on spruces, firs, and occasionally pines in areas with clean air and high humidity. It prefers the shaded, north-facing sides of trees in mature forests where the air stays consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: As snow melts and humidity increases, the lichen becomes more vibrant green and the powdery soredia at lobe tips are most visible and easily detected by touch.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods it appears more gray and subdued, but after summer rains it quickly transforms to a fresh green color within hours.
seasonality.fall: The contrast between the lichen's blue-gray color and the changing autumn foliage makes it easier to spot on tree trunks during forest walks.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round on bark, often appearing as blue-gray patches against snow-covered tree trunks, with the powdery tips still detectable under good lighting.

funFact: The powdery soredia at this lichen's lobe tips are actually tiny packages containing both fungal threads and algae cells - complete lichen starter kits that can blow away in the wind to establish new colonies miles away, making each speck of "powder" a potential new lichen waiting to happen!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other gray-green foliose lichens on conifers, but the consistently powdery, flour-like soredia at the lobe tips is diagnostic - if you can't easily rub off white powder from the lobe edges, it's probably a different species.
contextualKnowledge: **Note: This species is extremely rare in New England with only 2 documented observations.** This lichen is much more common in boreal regions of Canada and may be at the very southern edge of its range in northern New England, making any sightings particularly noteworthy for citizen science projects.
compareHints: As the only member of the Parmeliopsis genus documented in New England, compare it with similar shield lichens in the Parmelia family. Unlike common Parmelia species, Powder-tipped Starburst has soredia concentrated specifically at lobe tips rather than scattered across the surface, and it shows a strong preference for coniferous bark over the mixed substrates other shield lichens use.
